dna-rna-structure-s1.title: Which part of a cell extract changes harmless bacteria?
dna-rna-structure-s1.text: Strain S of a pneumonia bacterium makes a slippery outer capsule, forms smooth colonies and kills mice. Strain R makes no capsule, forms rough colonies and is harmless. Researchers killed S cells with heat, broke them open and made a cell-free extract. Portions of the extract were treated with one enzyme each, then mixed with live R cells in broth. After 6 hours, each culture was spread on plates and the colonies were counted (mean of three plates per tube).

table.caption: Colonies grown from R cells mixed with treated extracts of heat-killed S cells
cols: What was added to live R cells
rows: S extract treated with protease (destroys protein)
S extract treated with RNase (destroys RNA)
S extract treated with DNase (destroys DNA)
S extract treated with DNase that had first been boiled

dna-rna-structure-s2.title: Where the radioactive label goes when phages infect bacteria
dna-rna-structure-s2.text: A bacteriophage (phage) is a virus that infects bacteria. It is a protein coat with DNA inside. Researchers grew one batch of phages with radioactive sulfur (35S) and another with radioactive phosphorus (32P). Each batch infected E. coli cells for 10 minutes. The mixture was then spun in a blender to shake loose anything stuck to the outside of the cells, or left unblended, and centrifuged: the heavier cells formed a pellet at the bottom and free phage coats stayed in the liquid. Later, the new phages released from the infected cells were collected.

table.caption: Percent of each label found in each fraction
cols: Label recovered in new phages (% of what was added)

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the colony counts?
options: A molecule destroyed by DNase is needed to turn R cells into S cells.
A protein in the extract turns R cells into S cells, with some help from the RNA.
Heat-killed S cells came back to life in the tubes that grew S colonies.
The capsule itself, passed to R cells, makes them form S colonies.

why.correct: S colonies appear with untreated extract (46), protease-treated (44) and RNase-treated (49) extract, but not when DNA was destroyed (0). Only DNase removes the transforming activity, so DNA is the molecule required.
options: Correct: only the DNase treatment dropped S colonies to zero, matching the R-alone control.
Destroying protein left 44 S colonies, about the same as untreated extract, so protein is not required; RNase also left activity.
The extract was cell-free, and tube 5 had the same dead-cell material yet grew no S colonies; the change depends on DNA, not revival.
A capsule handed over would not be copied by dividing cells; colonies arise from many divisions, so the cells must have gained the ability to make capsules.

items.q: Why did the researchers include tube 6, with DNase that had been boiled before use?
options: To show that tube 5's result comes from the enzyme's activity, not from something else added with it
To show that boiling destroys the DNA in the S extract, so that no S colonies can form
To provide a second group of R cells alone so that the R colony counts can be averaged
To test whether boiled protein from the DNase preparation can itself turn R cells into S cells

why.correct: Boiling denatures the DNase but leaves everything else in the preparation. Tube 6 kept its S colonies (45), so tube 5's result was due to active DNase digesting DNA, not to a contaminant or the added protein.
options: Correct: it is a control that keeps every ingredient of tube 5 except the enzyme's activity.
The DNase, not the extract, was boiled; and tube 6 grew 45 S colonies, so the DNA in the extract still worked.
Tube 1 is the R-alone control; tube 6 contains S extract and DNase.
Boiled DNase is not a candidate transforming agent; it is there so the only difference from tube 5 is whether the enzyme works.

items.q: What percentage of all colonies on tube 2's plates are S-type? Give one decimal place.

why.correct: Total colonies = 2,950 + 46 = 2,996. S-type share = 46 ÷ 2,996 × 100 = 1.54%, which rounds to 1.5%. Transformation changes only a small fraction of the R cells.

items.q: Cells from one S-type colony in tube 2 are grown for 50 more generations in broth with no extract. Predict what their descendants will be like.
options: Nearly all make capsules: the capsule gene they took in is copied at every division
About half make capsules, because each division gives the new gene to one daughter cell
They lose their capsules within a few generations, because no extract is present to keep changing them
They make capsules for a while, then switch back to R as the original DNA takes over again

why.correct: Transformation is a heritable change: the DNA taken in becomes part of the cell's own genetic material and is copied before each division, so the descendants keep the S trait without more extract.
options: Correct: the gained DNA is passed on like the rest of the chromosome.
DNA is copied before division, so both daughter cells receive the gene; it is not split between them.
Once the DNA is part of the cell's genome, the trait does not depend on the extract still being present; this is the evidence that heredity changed.
Nothing removes the new DNA; S cells recovered from Griffith's mice stayed S when grown and injected again.

items.q: A critic argues that a little protein survived the protease in tube 3 and is the true transforming agent. Which further result would most weaken the critic's argument?
options: DNA purified until no protein can be detected transforms R cells as well, per microgram, as crude extract.
Tube 3 grew slightly fewer S colonies than tube 2, so protein might contribute a small part of the effect.
Mice injected with heat-killed S cells by themselves survive, so the dead cells do no harm without help.
Adding twice as much protease to the extract makes tube 3 grow the same number of R colonies as before.

why.correct: If protein were the agent, removing it should remove the activity. Highly purified DNA, with protein below detection, keeps full activity per microgram, so protein is not needed.
options: Correct: activity tracks the DNA, not the protein.
44 against 46 is within the plate-to-plate spread, and in any case it would not separate DNA from protein as the cause.
This is Griffith's control showing the dead cells alone are harmless; it says nothing about which molecule transforms.
R colony counts measure the R cells that grew, not transformation, and the critic's leftover protein could still be present.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the results for the blended samples?
options: Most of the <sup>32</sup>P stayed with the cells, while most of the <sup>35</sup>S came off into the liquid.
Most of the <sup>35</sup>S stayed with the cells, while most of the <sup>32</sup>P came off into the liquid.
Both labels split about evenly between the pellet and the liquid.
Both labels were found mostly in the new phages released from the cells.

why.correct: After blending, 79% of the <sup>32</sup>P was in the cell pellet, but 82% of the <sup>35</sup>S was in the liquid with the shaken-off coats.
options: Correct: phosphorus-labeled DNA went in; sulfur-labeled protein stayed outside.
This reverses the table: <sup>35</sup>S was 18% in the pellet and 82% in the liquid.
The splits are 18/82 and 79/21, far from even.
Only 31% of the <sup>32</sup>P and under 1% of the <sup>35</sup>S were recovered in new phages.

items.q: Why were sulfur and phosphorus chosen as the two labels?
options: Proteins contain sulfur but almost no phosphorus; DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur.
Sulfur labels the outside of a phage and phosphorus the inside, whatever molecules happen to be there.
Radioactive sulfur and phosphorus give off different colors, so the two can be told apart in one tube.
Both elements are found in DNA and in protein, so either label shows where the whole phage goes.

why.correct: Two of the twenty amino acids carry sulfur, and DNA has none; every DNA nucleotide carries a phosphate, and phage protein has essentially none. So <sup>35</sup>S tracks protein and <sup>32</sup>P tracks DNA.
options: Correct: the labels distinguish the two candidate molecules.
A label marks the molecules that contain the element, not a location; that is why the element had to differ between DNA and protein.
The batches were labeled and run separately; the choice of elements was about which molecules carry them.
If both molecules carried both elements, neither label could tell DNA from protein.

items.q: Even after blending, 18% of the <sup>35</sup>S was in the cell pellet. Which explanation is best supported by all the data?
options: Some empty coats stayed stuck to the cells; unblended samples show that coats stay on unless shaken off.
About a fifth of the phage protein entered the cells and then directed the making of the new phages.
Inside the cells, some <sup>35</sup>S was moved into DNA, so it stayed with the cell pellet.
Blending broke open some cells, releasing <sup>32</sup>P into the liquid and leaving <sup>35</sup>S behind.

why.correct: Without blending, 92% of the <sup>35</sup>S spun down with the cells, so attached coats pellet with them; blending removes most but not all. Protein that entered and acted would show up in new phages, but under 1% did.
options: Correct: incomplete removal of attached coats explains the pellet <sup>35</sup>S.
Protein that directed new phages would be found in them, but under 1% of the <sup>35</sup>S was recovered there.
DNA contains no sulfur, so <sup>35</sup>S cannot become part of DNA.
Broken cells would explain <sup>32</sup>P in the liquid, not <sup>35</sup>S in the pellet.

items.q: Suppose the researchers had labeled phages with radioactive carbon (<sup>14</sup>C) instead. Why could that experiment not tell which molecule carries the phage's genes?
options: Both DNA and protein contain carbon, so label would sit in both the coats and the injected material.
Bacteria do not take up carbon from the broth, so the phages grown in them would not become labeled.
Radioactive carbon kills the bacteria, so no new phages would be released.
Carbon atoms move from protein into DNA during infection, so the label would end up in DNA.

why.correct: A useful label must be in one candidate molecule and not the other. Every organic molecule contains carbon, so <sup>14</sup>C would be found in both the pellet and the liquid whatever entered the cell.
options: Correct: a label common to both molecules cannot separate them.
Bacteria build their molecules from the carbon in their food, so phages grown in them would be labeled; the problem is that every molecule would be.
Nothing suggests radioactive carbon would kill the cells; the design flaw is that it marks both molecules.
Even if some carbon were reused later, the label would start in both molecules, so it could not tell them apart.

items.q: Which conclusion does the last column (label recovered in new phages) best support?
options: The material the parent phage passes to its offspring is its DNA, not its protein coat.
New phages are built from the parent's coat protein, which is reused after infection.
The parent phage's DNA is broken down as soon as the cell starts to make new phages.
Phosphorus is used to build the coat proteins of the new phages.

why.correct: Almost a third of the parent's <sup>32</sup>P was passed on to the offspring phages, but under 1% of its <sup>35</sup>S. What passes from parent to offspring is DNA, as expected of hereditary material.
options: Correct: the parental DNA appears in the next generation.
Under 1% of the coat label reached the new phages, so the old coat is not reused.
31% of the parental <sup>32</sup>P turned up in the new phages, so the DNA was not all destroyed.
Protein contains almost no phosphorus; the <sup>32</sup>P in the new phages is in their DNA.

items.q: In double-stranded DNA, each base pair is made of
options: one purine and one pyrimidine
two purines, joined by hydrogen bonds
two pyrimidines, joined by hydrogen bonds
a purine or pyrimidine and a phosphate group

why.correct: A (a purine) pairs with T (a pyrimidine), and G (a purine) pairs with C (a pyrimidine).
options: Correct: every rung combines a two-ring base and a one-ring base.
Two two-ring bases would be too long to fit between the backbones.
Two one-ring bases would be too short to reach each other and bond.
Phosphates are in the backbone; a base pair is two bases.

items.q: Imagine a form of DNA in which adenine paired with guanine and cytosine paired with thymine, with the same backbones. Predict how its double helix would differ from real DNA.
options: Its width would change along its length, wide at A–G pairs and narrow at C–T pairs.
Its width would stay the same everywhere, but it would be held by fewer hydrogen bonds.
Its two strands would run in the same direction instead of opposite directions.
It would contain more purines than pyrimidines in each of its two strands.

why.correct: A and G are both purines (two rings), C and T both pyrimidines (one ring). Purine–purine rungs would be long and pyrimidine–pyrimidine rungs short, so the helix would bulge and pinch instead of keeping a uniform width.
options: Correct: uniform width depends on every pair being one purine plus one pyrimidine.
The width would not stay the same, because the rungs would have two different lengths.
Strand direction is set by the backbone chemistry, which the question keeps the same.
A strand can have any mix of bases; pairing rules constrain the two strands together, so this does not follow.

items.q: A double-stranded DNA molecule is 5,000 base pairs long and contains 1,400 cytosine bases. How many adenine bases does it contain? Give a whole number.
Which features describe the DNA of a typical bacterium such as E. coli? Select all that apply.
options: A single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm
Small extra circles of DNA (plasmids) that can carry a few genes
Several linear chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope
DNA wound around histones into nucleosomes
A separate chromosome for each of its genes

why.correct: A bacterium has no nucleus. Its main DNA is one circular chromosome in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and many carry plasmids as well.
options: Correct: one circular chromosome, with no nuclear envelope around it.
Correct: plasmids are common, and their genes (for example for surviving a drug) can be useful.
Several linear chromosomes in a nucleus describe a eukaryote.
Histones and nucleosomes package eukaryotic DNA; bacteria fold their DNA with other proteins.
One chromosome carries thousands of genes; a cell does not hold one chromosome per gene.

items.q: In fruit flies, a chromosome rearrangement moved a normally active eye-color gene next to a block of tightly packed chromatin. In many eye cells the gene's protein was no longer made, though its base sequence was unchanged. Which explanation is best?
options: Tight packing spread into the moved gene, so the proteins that read genes could no longer reach its DNA.
The move cut the gene's DNA into pieces, so no complete copy of it was left in those cells.
The tightly packed region changed the gene's base sequence to one that codes for a different protein.
The gene was moved out of the nucleus, so it now sits in the cytoplasm of those cells.

why.correct: In heterochromatin the DNA is wound so tightly that the proteins that read genes mostly cannot bind. When that packing spreads into a neighboring gene, the gene is silenced in the cells where it spreads, with no change in sequence.
options: Correct: packing controls access, so the same gene can be on or off.
The stem says the sequence is unchanged, and a gene in pieces would not be fully restored in other cells.
Packing changes how accessible DNA is, not its base sequence; the stem rules out a sequence change.
Chromosomes stay in the nucleus; the gene moved along the chromosomes, not out of the nucleus.

items.q: Histone proteins carry many amino acids with positively charged side chains, such as lysine and arginine. How does this help histones package DNA?
options: The positive charges attract DNA's negatively charged phosphate groups along the backbone.
The positive charges pair with the bases in the middle of the helix, holding the strands together.
The positive charges repel the DNA, pushing it into a tightly folded shape.
The positive charges form covalent bonds with the sugars in DNA's backbone.

why.correct: Each nucleotide's phosphate carries a negative charge, so DNA's outside is strongly negative. Positively charged side chains attract it, letting the DNA wrap tightly around the histone core.
options: Correct: opposite charges attract (ionic interactions).
The bases pair with each other inside the helix; histones contact the backbone on the outside.
Repulsion would push DNA away from histones, not wrap it around them.
The attraction is ionic and can loosen when charges change; histones do not bond covalently to the sugars.

items.q: In Griffith's 1928 experiments with mice, which observation is the evidence that something passed from dead S cells to live R cells?
options: Live S bacteria were recovered from mice given heat-killed S cells plus live R cells.
Mice injected with live S cells died, while mice injected with live R cells survived.
Mice injected with heat-killed S cells by themselves survived the injection.
Mice injected with a mix of heat-killed S cells and live R cells showed signs of pneumonia.

why.correct: Only live R cells were injected alive, yet live S cells came out. R cells must have gained the S trait from the dead cells, and kept it as they multiplied.
options: Correct: live S cells appeared where only dead S cells had gone in.
This only shows that S is deadly and R is not; it is the starting point, not evidence of transfer.
This control shows the dead S cells alone are harmless, but nothing passes anywhere in it.
Sickness alone could mean the dead cells harmed the mice with help from R; recovering live S cells is what shows the R cells changed.

items.q: A drug causes the chromatin in a cell's nucleus to loosen into a more open form. Compared with an untreated cell, predict each quantity.

variables.name: Number of genes whose DNA the gene-reading proteins can reach
variables.why: Looser chromatin (more like euchromatin) exposes more DNA to the proteins that read genes.

variables.name: Total amount of DNA in the nucleus
variables.why: Loosening changes how the DNA is packed, not how much DNA there is.

variables.name: Share of the chromatin that is tightly packed heterochromatin
variables.why: The drug opens chromatin, so less of it stays in the tightly packed form.

variables.name: Base sequence of each gene
variables.why: Packing affects access to DNA, not the order of its bases.

why.correct: Packing controls access. Opening the chromatin lets the proteins that read genes reach more DNA and shrinks the heterochromatin, but the amount of DNA and its sequence stay the same.

items.q: Put the levels of DNA packing in a eukaryotic cell in order, from least to most compact.
options: The double helix by itself, 2 nm wide
DNA wrapped around histones as nucleosomes, like beads on a string
The string of nucleosomes coiled into a thicker fiber
The fiber folded into loops attached to a protein scaffold
A fully condensed chromosome during mitosis

why.correct: Each level folds the one before it: the helix wraps histones, nucleosomes coil into a fiber, the fiber folds into loops, and in mitosis the loops condense into the compact chromosome you can see under a light microscope.

items.q: Which result would best support the claim that RNA, not protein, is the hereditary material of a plant virus?
options: RNA purified from the virus, free of protein, infects leaves, and complete new viruses form.
The virus particles are made of an RNA molecule wrapped in a coat of protein subunits.
Infected leaves contain more RNA than healthy leaves of the same size and age from the same plant.
The virus's RNA is a single strand, while the plant's own DNA is a double strand.

why.correct: If RNA by itself can start an infection that produces whole new viruses, coat and all, then the RNA carries the instructions; this was shown for tobacco mosaic virus in the 1950s.
options: Correct: the RNA alone is sufficient to make complete offspring viruses.
This describes what the particle contains, not which part carries the instructions.
More RNA in sick leaves could come from the plant's own response; it does not test which molecule is hereditary.
Being single-stranded says nothing about whether the molecule carries the hereditary instructions.
